presentation: Knee extension weakness and L3-L4 root
stem:
A 58-year-old man has had two weeks of pain across the front of his thigh and inner shin. On examination he cannot fully straighten his right knee against resistance, the right knee jerk is reduced, and the ankle jerk and ankle movements are normal. MRI is arranged to look for nerve root compression.

Which nerve root is most likely to be affected?

options.A: L5 root, as in a typical sciatic-type disc prolapse
options.B: L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
options.C: S1 root, supplying the calf muscles
options.E: L1 root, supplying the hip flexor muscles

correct_answer: B. L3 and L4 roots, supplying the quadriceps
why_correct: Straightening the knee depends on the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve from the L3 and L4 roots, and the knee jerk is mediated by the same roots. Weak knee extension with a reduced knee jerk and normal ankle findings therefore localises to L3-L4. Source: Standard myotome and reflex levels, Medical Research Council scale and UK undergraduate clinical neurology teaching.
why_wrong: A. L5 mainly controls ankle and big-toe dorsiflexion and hip abduction, and does not explain the weak knee extension or the reduced knee jerk. C. S1 supplies plantarflexion and the ankle jerk, which are normal here. D. The hamstrings bend the knee rather than straighten it, so S2 does not fit. E. L1 contributes to hip flexion and groin sensation, not to the quadriceps.
pearl: Knee jerk is L3-L4 and ankle jerk is S1-S2; matching the reflex to the weak movement fixes the level.
thinking: Weak knee extension  ↓  quadriceps / femoral nerve  ↓  knee jerk reduced  ↓  root level L3-L4
exam_trap: Choosing L5 because it is the commonest lumbar root in sciatica, when the weakness is at the knee and the ankle examination is normal.
takeaway: Knee extension and the knee jerk are L3-L4; ankle dorsiflexion is L4-L5 and the ankle jerk is S1.
notes: Source was a one-line recall item; rebuilt as a root-localisation vignette (root compression) rather than a nerve-name question, so it does not repeat BX643 (femoral nerve after pelvic surgery). Source key L3-L4 is correct. No guideline exists for myotome levels; citation is standard teaching.
sources: Standard myotome/reflex tables (MRC); clinical neurological examination teaching

notes: Duplicate: live BX173 (wasting/fasciculations with reduced reflexes = LMN), BX637 and BX641 already test LMN vs UMN signs.

stem:
A 29-year-old woman with a three-year history of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis develops numbness and clumsiness of her left hand over four days. She has no fever or urinary symptoms. Over the next six weeks the symptoms improve substantially without full recovery of fine finger movements.

Which term best describes this episode?
correct_answer: B. Relapse of her multiple sclerosis
why_correct: A relapse in multiple sclerosis is a new or worsening neurological episode that develops over days, lasts longer than a brief fluctuation, occurs without fever or infection, and is followed by full or partial recovery. This woman's established diagnosis, afebrile subacute onset and later improvement fit that pattern. Source: NICE NG220, Multiple sclerosis in adults: management, 2022.
why_wrong: A. Clinically isolated syndrome describes the first demyelinating episode before multiple sclerosis is diagnosed, and she already has the diagnosis. C. A pseudorelapse is a temporary worsening of old symptoms triggered by infection or heat, but she has no fever or infective symptoms. D. A primary progressive course shows steady worsening from onset without distinct episodes and recovery. E. Nothing suggests a functional cause, and an established demyelinating disease explains the deficit.
pearl: After a presumed relapse, always look for infection or fever first, because pseudorelapses mimic relapses.
thinking: Known relapsing-remitting MS  ↓  new symptoms over days  ↓  no infection or fever  ↓  partial recovery = relapse
exam_trap: Calling it a clinically isolated syndrome, which is only used for the first episode before the diagnosis is made.
takeaway: A relapse is new or worsening MS symptoms over days, without infection, usually followed by recovery.
notes: One-line term-recall item rebuilt as a vignette. Wording avoids any duration threshold (NG220 uses more than 24 hours and 30 days from the last relapse; not needed for the key). Does not repeat NEU019 (relapse treatment) or DS004 (excluding infection first).
Duplicate: live NEU066 (MS with episodes separated in time and place) tests the same diagnosis and learning point.

stem:
A 66-year-old man is recently diagnosed with Parkinson's disease after developing a resting tremor and slowness of movement. He asks his GP whether other problems he noticed for years before the tremor could be part of the same condition.

Which of his earlier symptoms is a recognised non-motor feature of Parkinson's disease?

options.A: Episodes of pleuritic chest pain on deep breathing
options.B: Recurrent painful swelling of the knee joints
options.C: A progressively reduced sense of smell
options.D: Gradually worsening difficulty with night vision
options.E: Frequent unprovoked nosebleeds from one nostril

correct_answer: C. A progressively reduced sense of smell
why_correct: Parkinson's disease has many non-motor features, and a reduced sense of smell (hyposmia) is among the commonest and may precede the tremor by years. Others include constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder, low mood and autonomic problems, which is why symptoms outside movement should be asked about. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, 2017.
why_wrong: A. Pleuritic chest pain suggests a pleural or pericardial problem and is not part of Parkinson's disease. B. Recurrent joint swelling points to an inflammatory or crystal arthropathy. D. Poor night vision suggests retinal or vitamin A-related disease, not Parkinson's disease. E. Unilateral recurrent epistaxis needs a local nasal cause to be sought.
pearl: Hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behaviour disorder and low mood can precede the motor features of Parkinson's disease.
thinking: Parkinson's disease diagnosed  ↓  ask about non-motor symptoms  ↓  smell loss, constipation, sleep disorder, mood  ↓  choose the recognised feature
exam_trap: Thinking Parkinson's disease only affects movement, so that a loss of smell is dismissed as an unrelated problem.
takeaway: Parkinson's disease has recognised non-motor features such as hyposmia, constipation and sleep disturbance.
notes: Source distractors (haematemesis, jaundice etc.) were trivially wrong; replaced with distractors of similar length. Source key was constipation; this version tests hyposmia so it does not clash with the constipation items already live. PAN1905 skipped as the same learning point. Not repeating NEU062 (RBD) or PAQ15228 (volvulus).
Duplicate within my own set: same learning point (non-motor features of Parkinson's disease) as PAN10581, which I wrote.
Duplicate: live BX885 (length-dependent sensory loss with reduced ankle reflexes) tests the peripheral neuropathy pattern.
Duplicate: live END029 and PAQ16049 already test burning symmetrical foot symptoms in diabetes = diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Duplicate: live END059, END029 and PAQ16049 cover stocking-distribution diabetic neuropathy.
Duplicate: live BX577 (neurological features of B12 deficiency) tests the same learning point.
Duplicate: live BX885 (length-dependent distal sensory symptoms) tests the same learning point; PAN2228 covers alcohol-related neuropathy.

stem:
A 35-year-old man with known epilepsy has a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure at home. When paramedics arrive, his left arm and leg are weak. His weakness gradually improves over several hours and has fully resolved by the next morning. A CT head scan is normal.

What is the most likely explanation for the weakness?

options.E: Acute demyelination of the right hemisphere

why_correct: Temporary focal weakness lasting minutes to hours after a seizure is Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis), thought to reflect neuronal exhaustion in the area that seized. It resolves spontaneously, and a normal scan with a clear temporal relationship to a witnessed seizure supports it. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. A transient ischaemic attack can cause temporary weakness, but here the weakness began straight after a convulsion and evolved gradually, which points to a postictal cause. B. Hemiplegic migraine follows a headache and aura rather than a generalised convulsion. C. Functional weakness is a diagnosis of exclusion and is not suggested by a witnessed seizure in a known epileptic. E. Demyelination evolves over days and does not resolve within hours.
pearl: Todd's paresis lasts from minutes to a day or so; persistent weakness should prompt imaging for stroke or other structural causes.
thinking: Known epilepsy and witnessed seizure  ↓  hemiparesis afterwards  ↓  improves over hours  ↓  Todd's paresis
exam_trap: Labelling post-seizure weakness as a stroke or TIA without recognising the postictal pattern.
takeaway: Transient focal weakness after a seizure that resolves over hours is Todd's paresis.
notes: Source distractors were unrelated diagnoses; replaced with plausible competing causes of transient hemiweakness. Plan puts the key at D. NG217 does not name Todd's paresis explicitly; citation is for the epilepsy context, the term is standard neurology teaching.
Duplicate: live NEU074 and NEU037 already test Lambert-Eaton syndrome (proximal weakness plus dry mouth).
Duplicate: live PAQ15927 (proximal weakness with normal sensation = myopathy) and RHE020 cover the same learning point.
Duplicate: live NEU022 and NEU055 already test fatigable ptosis = myasthenia gravis.
Duplicate: live NEU081 and NEU034 test miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis = Horner syndrome.
Duplicate: live NEU022/NEU055 test fatigable ptosis and diplopia = myasthenia gravis (fatigable weakness).
Duplicate: live DS034 tests thymus imaging/thymoma association in newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman has 2 months of drooping of the left upper eyelid and double vision that are worse in the evening and improve after rest. A colleague wonders whether this is a third cranial nerve palsy.

Which finding would most strongly suggest a third nerve palsy and argue against myasthenia gravis?

options.A: Ptosis that worsens during sustained upward gaze
options.B: Improvement of the ptosis after a short rest
options.C: Double vision that is worse at the end of the day
options.D: Normal pupillary reactions to light bilaterally
options.E: A dilated left pupil that reacts poorly to light

correct_answer: E. A dilated left pupil that reacts poorly to light
why_correct: Myasthenia gravis affects the neuromuscular junction of the extraocular and levator muscles but does not involve the smooth muscle that controls the pupil, so pupils stay normal. A dilated, poorly reactive pupil implies parasympathetic involvement from a compressive or other third nerve lesion and should prompt urgent assessment and imaging. Source: Standard UK clinical neurology teaching on ptosis and diplopia (Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine).
why_wrong: A. Worsening ptosis on prolonged upgaze is the fatigability seen in myasthenia gravis. B. Improvement with rest is typical of myasthenia gravis. C. Evening worsening of diplopia is the usual diurnal pattern of myasthenia gravis. D. Normal pupils are expected in myasthenia gravis and would not point towards a third nerve palsy.
pearl: A dilated pupil with ptosis and double vision needs urgent imaging to look for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
thinking: Ptosis and diplopia  ↓  fatigability and normal pupils = neuromuscular junction  ↓  abnormal dilated pupil = third nerve lesion
exam_trap: Assuming all ptosis with diplopia is myasthenia gravis, when an involved pupil changes the diagnosis and urgency.
takeaway: Myasthenia gravis spares the pupil, so an abnormal pupil with ptosis suggests a third nerve lesion.
notes: Re-angled the 'pupils usually spared' recall item as a discriminating-finding question (same learning point). PAN10572 skipped as the same learning point within this writer's set. No single guideline; classic neurology teaching - please confirm or replace the citation at review. Not duplicating NEU022.
sources: Standard UK clinical neurology teaching; Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine

notes: Duplicate within my own set: same learning point (pupils spared in myasthenia gravis) as PAN3915, which I wrote.

stem:
A 24-year-old man has a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure at a party. The convulsive movements stop after about a minute. Over the next 20 minutes he is drowsy and confused, does not recognise his friends and has a headache, before gradually returning to normal.

Which term describes the period after the convulsive movements stopped?
why_correct: The postictal phase is the recovery period after a seizure, in which drowsiness, confusion, headache and sometimes transient focal weakness are common. It follows the ictal phase (the seizure itself) and gradually resolves. Source: NICE NG217, Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, 2022.
why_wrong: A. An aura is a focal seizure symptom experienced at the start of a seizure, before the convulsion. B. The prodromal phase is the vague change in mood or behaviour that can occur hours or days before a seizure. D. The interictal period is the time between seizures when the person is clinically well. E. The ictal phase is the seizure itself, which had ended.
pearl: Prolonged postictal confusion beyond the expected recovery period should prompt a search for non-convulsive status epilepticus or another cause.
thinking: Convulsion stopped  ↓  drowsy, confused, headache  ↓  recovering state  ↓  postictal phase
exam_trap: Choosing ictal because the patient is still unwell, when the seizure activity itself has ended.
takeaway: Drowsiness and confusion after a seizure define the postictal phase.
notes: Source key was postictal state (position E); re-ordered to plan letter C. Terminology recall rebuilt with a vignette. NG217 does not define the phases; term is standard teaching.
Duplicate: live NEU015 (first unprovoked seizure -> first-seizure clinic) and PAAKT043 test the same learning point.
Duplicate: live NEU042 and ACU047 (first-line benzodiazepine for status epilepticus) test the same learning point.
Duplicate: live ACU047, NEU042 and NEU001 (status epilepticus after several minutes of seizure) test the same learning point.
